# Bayesian reasoning {#sec-bayes}

::: {.aside}
`r paste(readLines("_Words/chap_12.txt"), collapse = "\n")` 
:::

We are in the midst of a real-world experiment involving millions of people in a life-or-death situation. Perhaps that is an overly dramatic description. The experiment we have in mind concerns the testing of self-driving taxis in urban areas. Companies like Waymo have deployed fleets of self-driving cars that offer a taxi service. 

That such testing is allowed is itself notable. How much experience will we need with the cars to be sure that we are making a proper judgment? 

## An uncertain situation



Companies currently run pilot programs deploying self-driving taxis in a handful of cities. They have already collected substantial amounts of data and reported summaries such as this [Waymo bulletin](https://waymo.com/blog/2023/12/waymo-significantly-outperforms-comparable-human-benchmarks-over-7-million). Instead of commenting on this data, let us imagine ourselves at the time when the safety experiment is just beginning. Then, we will gradually accumulate data to form and update our beliefs about fleet safety. We will keep it realistic, but because the data will be made-up, do not use this example to draw conclusions about the real world.

`r qr_margin_note(
  "https://waymo.com/blog/2023/12/waymo-significantly-outperforms-comparable-human-benchmarks-over-7-million",
  "Waymo bulletin"
)`

"Safety" is a dimension, an aspect of the transportation system. Modeling safety starts by defining it clearly, to *operationalize* it. Our operationalization in this discussion will be the *number of miles driven* by each car from the time it enters service until the first accident.  We can define an "accident" as an incident that generates a claim on insurance or requires a police report. For other purposes, a different operationalization might be appropriate, for instance the number of close calls or near-misses

A car without an accident to date is not necessarily safe. Even accident-free cars provide information about fleet safety; the duration of the no-accident-yet interval carries that information. (See `r xf("fig-likelihood-curve")`.) A car that goes a large number of miles without an accident provides pro-safety evidence; A car that has an accident after a small number of miles does the opposite.

Chance influences whether a car is in an accident. This play of chance can be modeled with a probability distribution. An appropriate family of distributions for this was used earlier in `r xf("sec-hypothesis-and-likelihood")`: the exponential family. In `r xf("sec-hypothesis-and-likelihood")` we used the *time* between incidents. For driving, the mileage of each car is a better representation of that car's exposure to the risk of accidents. 

Exponential distributions model the time interval, or mileage, in our case, between incidents. The interval here is the mileage from the start of the experiment until the first accident. For an individual car, this interval is modeled as random, a draw from the exponential distribution used to model the individual cars.

Even though each accident (or lack of accident) is random, the fleet safety plays a role. This fleet-level safety is operationalized by the particular *rate* parameter used for the individual-car randomness. The appropriate value for the  *rate* parameter is uncertain. This uncertainty is large at the start of the experiment. As the experiment proceeds and more data arrives, the uncertainty will decrease.

## The fleet-wide likelihood function

Fleet-safety uncertainty is a probability distribution on the *rate* parameter itself. Unlike individual-car uncertainty, this need not be exponential in form. At first, we don't even know the proper form for the distribution should be. We will have to discover that form as we go along.

Suppose that at the end of each month the mileage and accident status of every car in the fleet are recorded. For any assumed value of the rate parameter, the likelihood of the observed data can be computed: multiply together the likelihoods for each individual car's observed outcome.

The rate parameter is uncertain. Repeating the likelihood calculation for each possible value of the *rate* allows us to see how plausible each value is given the observed data. In other words, we create a *likelihood function* for the rate parameter.

Imagine that you are the person responsible for constructing the likelihood function that incorporates the latest data. You have a stack of cards, each recording the current mileage of an individual car or, if the car had an accident, the mileage at which the accident occurred. Each card's information corresponds to an individual likelihood function for that car.

Plotting the individual-car likelihood functions requires choosing appropriate range of values for the rate parameter. Historical data on human-driven cars suggests a rate of about five serious accidents per million vehicle miles. A sensible plotting range is 0 to 40 accidents per million miles. The upper end lets you consider hypothetically very dangerous cars. The low end hypothesizes that self-driving cars are safer than human-driven. The middle hypothesizes that self-driving cars are about as safe as human-driven cars. `r xf("fig-individual-cars")` shows three individual-car likelihood functions based on the most recent data for that car. The cars plotted in panels (a) and (c) have not yet had an accident. The car in (b) had an accident at mileage 78,954.


```{r}
#| label: fig-individual-cars
#| echo: false
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| fig.cap: "Individual likelihood functions for several cars based on their mileage and accident status."
#| fig.subcap:
#| - 31,448 miles with no accident
#| - 78,954 miles with an accident
#| - 54,365 miles with no accident
dom <- domain(rate = 0:40)

Pa <- slice_plot(1-pexp(31448, rate/1e6) ~ rate, dom, color = .slice_color.) |>
  gf_labs(x = "Hypothesized rate (per million miles)", 
  y = "Individual-car likelihood") |>
  gf_lims(y = c(0,1)) |>
  gf_hline(yintercept = 0.1, color=.hline_color.)

Pb <- slice_plot(dexp(78954, rate/1e6) ~ rate, dom, color = .slice_color.) |>
    gf_labs(x = "Hypothesized rate (per million miles)", 
    y = "Individual-car likelihood") |>
    gf_hline(yintercept = 0.46e-6, color=.hline_color.)

Pc <- slice_plot(1 - pexp(54365, rate/1e6) ~ rate, dom, color = .slice_color.) |>
    gf_labs(x = "Hypothesized rate (per million miles)", 
    y = "Individual-car likelihood") |>
  gf_lims(y = c(0,1)) |>
  gf_hline(yintercept = 0.1, color=.hline_color.)

  Pa
  Pb
  Pc
```

Consider the likelihood functions graphed in `r xf("fig-individual-cars")`. The two accident-free cars' likelihood functions differ only slightly in shape. 

The accident-free cars favor a low hypothesized rate parameter. Their likelihood functions peak at a rate of 0 accidents per million miles and fall steadily as the hypothesized rate increases. This evidence hardly proves that the cars are safe. Recall that a likelihood ratio of 10 is only "limited evidence" in favor of the more likely hypothesis. (See `r xf("tbl-likelihood-ratio-verbal")`.) Only hypothesized rates where the likelihood falls *below* the [magenta]{style="color: magenta;"} can be considered unlikely. So the accident-free cars don't rule out a very high hypothesized rate of 40 accidents per million miles. This isn't surprising, since the rate 40 per million miles amounts to an average of one accident every 25,000 miles! Reaching 54,000 miles isn't shocking even under high risk.

The car in panel (b) experienced an accident. Its likelihood function has an argmax at a hypothesized rate of 12.7 accidents per million miles. This means an average of one accident every 80,000 miles, entirely consistent with the car having had an accident at 78,954 miles. This car only weakly argues against rates below 0.5 accidents per million miles.

Any individual car's evidence does not precisely identify a specific hypothesized rate parameter. Each car here is entirely consistent with the historical rate for human-driven cars.

But your job is not yet complete. Combine the evidence from all the individual cars to assess what they have to say about fleet safety. Fortunately, this is easy. Just multiply the functions together. The result, from just these three cars is shown in `r xf("fig-combined-cars")`.

```{r}
#| label: fig-combined-cars
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Combined likelihood for all three cars"
slice_plot(dexp(78954, rate/1e6)*
(1-pexp(54365, rate/1e6)*(1-pexp(31448, rate/1e6))) ~ rate, 
      domain(rate=0:40), color = .slice_color.) |>
    gf_labs(x = "Hypothesized rate (per million miles)", 
    y = "Individual-car likelihood") |>
    gf_hline(yintercept = 0.44e-6, color=.hline_color.)
```

Data from just three cars cannot resolve whether the self-driving cars are safer or more dangerous than human-driven cars. You need data from hundreds or perhaps thousands of cars.

Since individual-car likelihoods are weak on their own, you decide to adopt a work flow where, as you pick up each car's data card, you immediately update the combined likelihood, by multiplying it by the new card's likelihood. 

## The Prior

There's a small technical glitch to take care of. The first card has no combined likelihood to multiply it with. Two simple work-arounds are available: 

a. Use the likelihood function from the first card as the initial combined likelihood.

b. Start with a combined likelihood function of that is uniform, which effectively says "I have no prior evidence for one hypothesized rate over another." 

Note that (a) and (b) amount to the same thing. In practice you are starting out with the likelihood function from the first card. But designers already did substantial work to make the cars safe.  For instance, the government approved the test cars for use on the public roads in the first place.

The Bayesian framework has a slot for inserting such before-the-first-data-card knowledge into the analysis. This is called the `r xf_definition("prior")` and reflects what you know *before* looking at the data. The "you" here is important. The experiment aims to convince others, no just yourself, that enough evidence exists for a meaningful conclusion. So the prior should reflect the beliefs of both the skeptic and the enthusiast.

US Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg had a helpful view about debate. She said, "Fight for the things that you care about, but do it in a way that will lead others to join you." One way to lead others to join you is to acknowledge the possibility that they might be right. In the Bayesian framework, this means broadening your prior to support the views of all (reasonable) people engaged in the debate. You do not have to assign much probability to those views, but you must assign some.

Sensible priors should be broad, not narrow minded. This point is not unique to quantitative analysis, but applies to reasoning and debate more generally.

> *To have doubted one's own first principles is the mark of a civilized man.* --- Supreme Court Justice, Oliver Wendell Holmes, Jr (1841-1935)

> *Doubt is an uncomfortable condition, but certainty is a ridiculous one.* --- Voltaire (1694-1778)

> *The whole problem with the world is that fools and fanatics are always so certain of themselves, and wiser people so full of doubts.* --- Bertrand Russell (1872-1970)

## The Posterior and Bayesian updating {#sec-posterior}

Let's re-consider the work-flow presented in the previous section. You started with an appropriately vague prior, then multiplied it successively by the likelihood from each data card as you picked it up. In the end, you have a distribution that reflects all the data. This distribution is called the `r xf_definition("posterior")`, the state of your knowledge after taking all the data into account. 

Calling the likelihood function from the first card L_1_() and so on for the subsequent cards, the posterior distribution after n cards is:

posterior() $\equiv$ prior() $\times$ L_1_() $\times$ L_2_() $\times$ ... $\times$ L_n_()

Since the prior() in the previous section was vague, perhaps even `flat()`, it's reasonable to wonder why even to give it a name; just multiply the cards' likelihood functions together. Indeed, for a hundred years statistical theory was dominated by exactly this point of view, named "Frequentist statistics." 

Consider, however, a slightly different scenario for processing the data on vehicle mileage and accidents. Rather than a batch of cards coming in all at once, suppose that they arrive sequentially, one by one. For the sake of definiteness, let's assume that they arrive once per day and that the likelihood function for each day's data is L_day_(). 

On day zero, before any cards arrive, all you have is your vague prior, which we'll call prior_0_(). In comes the first card, day 1, and you perform your calculation, multiplying that day's likelihood by the prior:

posterior_1() $\equiv L_1_() $\times$ prior_0_()

On day two, the second card arrives. The Bayesian multiplication for day two will be

posterior_2() $\equiv L_2_() $\times$ posterior_1_()

And for day three:

posterior_3() $\equiv L_3_() $\times$ posterior_2_()

The general pattern is that yesterday's posterior becomes today's prior. The prior is your state of knowledge in the morning. The posterior is your state of knowledge after the day's work is done.

Even if prior_0_() is vague, the prior for successive days will become less and less vague as more data is incorporated.

## Example: A ship in trouble


```{r}
#| echo: false
mu <- c(0.5, 0.7)
Sigma <- matrix(c(1, 0.75,
                   0.75, 1.2), nrow = 2)

mu2 <- c(-0.3, -0.5)
Sigma2 <- matrix(c(1.3, -0.75,
                   -0.75, 0.9), nrow = 2)

Grid <- expand.grid(x1 = seq(-3, 3, length.out = 100),
                     x2 = seq(-3, 3, length.out = 100))

                     direction1 <- function(Grid, center = c(-8, 8)) {
  angle <- atan2(Grid$x2 - center[2], Grid$x1 - center[1]) * 180 / pi
  dnorm(angle, -46, 2) + 2*dnorm(angle, -41, 5)
}
Grid$angle1 <- direction1(Grid)

direction2 <- function(Grid, center = c(8, 8)) {
  angle <- atan2(Grid$x2 - center[2], Grid$x1 - center[1]) * 180 / pi
  dnorm(angle, -137, 2) + dnorm(angle, -132, 4)
}
Grid$angle2 <- direction2(Grid)

Grid$density <- Grid$angle1 * Grid$angle2

# Grid$density <- (dmvnorm(Grid, mean = mu, sigma = Sigma) + dmvnorm(Grid, mean = mu2, sigma = Sigma2))


plane_fun <- function(Grid, center = c(0,0), angle = 45) { #degrees
  y <- Grid[[2]] - center[2]
  x <- Grid[[1]] - center[2]
  new_angle <- atan2(y, x) - angle * pi / 180
  offset <- sqrt(x^2 + y^2) * abs(sin(new_angle))
  dnorm(offset, 0, 0.5)
}

Grid$plane_prob <- plane_fun(Grid, c(0,0), 45)
Grid$posterior <- 1

SOS_location = c(0, 0)
SOS_Sigma <- matrix(c(3, 0,
                      0, 3), nrow = 2)
Grid$SOS <- dmvnorm(Grid [, c(1,2)], mean = SOS_location, sigma = SOS_Sigma)

```

A small ship sets out to sea, but the transponder that tracks its location fails on the second day. By the fourth day of the voyage, the ship's position is largely unknown. It's reasonable to model the uncertainty in location as a uniform probability distribution over a wide region. This constitutes the prior, drawn in `r xf("fig-ship-prior")`.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ship-prior
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Prior for the ship's location on the evening of day four. The uniform nature of the prior reflects complete uncertainty about where the ship might be in this patch of the ocean."
Grid2 <- expand.grid(x1 = seq(-3, 3, length.out = 100),
                     x2 = seq(-3, 3, length.out = 100))
Grid2$prior <- dnorm(sqrt(Grid2$x1^2 + Grid2$x2^2), 0, 12)
Grid2$prior[1] <- 0
ggplot(Grid2, aes(x = x1, y = x2, z = prior)) +
  geom_contour_filled(alpha = 0.5) +
  coord_fixed() +
  xlab("Longitude (deg)") + 
  ylab("Latitude (deg)") + guides(fill = "none", color="none")
```

Unhappily, a fire erupts onboard the ship on the evening of day four. The crew has mere moments to send a brief SOS message. 

The SOS is received by far-away radio stations on land. Being so brief, the SOS message text doesn't state the ship's latitude and longitude. Fortunately, however, the radio receivers on land are *directional*, that is, they can trace the approximate direction from which the signal comes. This provides location information but comes with substantial uncertainty. This uncertainty can be modeled with a likelihood function. 

That likelihood function takes as input a hypothesized location for the ship. With a given location---even though it is merely a hypothesis---the direction to each of the two receiving stations can be exactly determined. In general, this won't be an exact match to the Coast Guards radio direction-finding data. To the extent that the calculated hypothetical direction matches the observed one, the likelihood is higher. By repeating the calculation for many different hypothesized locations a likelihood *function* can be established. `r xf("fig-direction-likelihoods")` displays this calculated function.

```{r echo=FALSE}
#| label: fig-direction-likelihoods
#| fig-cap: "Location likelihood for the individual direction-finding stations"
#| fig-subcap: 
#| - Station 1
#| - Station 2
ggplot(Grid, aes(x = x1, y = x2, z = angle1)) +
  geom_contour_filled(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_contour(color = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  guides(fill = "none", color="none") + 
  coord_fixed() +
  xlab("Longitude (deg)") + 
  ylab("Latitude (deg)")  

ggplot(Grid, aes(x = x1, y = x2, z = angle2)) +
  geom_contour_filled(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_contour(color = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  guides(fill = "none", color="none") + 
  coord_fixed() +
  xlab("Longitude (deg)") + 
  ylab("Latitude (deg)")   
```


Remember that the prior distribution reflects the initial ignorance of the ship's location. The direction-finding likelihoods narrow this down. 

Multiplying the prior by the likelihood for Station 1 and the likelihood for Station 2 gives the posterior shown in `r xf("fig-ship-location")`.


```{r}
#| label: fig-ship-location
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-cap-location: top
#| fig-cap: "Posterior probability for the ship's location based on the original prior and both directional measurements."
ggplot(Grid, aes(x = x1, y = x2, z = density)) +
  geom_contour_filled(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_contour(color = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  guides(fill = "none", color="none") + 
  coord_fixed() +
  xlab("Longitude (deg)") + 
  ylab("Latitude (deg)")   
```

Anxious to find the ship's crew, one of the Coast Guard stations sends out a search and rescue plane. It flies in a straight line toward the most likely location in `r xf("fig-ship-posterior1")`(b). 

It can be hard to spot a life raft from a quick-moving plane. Again, based on the plane's course and the Coast Guard's experience they can construct a likelihood for the plane's finding the raft. This is graphed in `r xf("fig-plane-likelihood")`.

```{r}
#| label: fig-plane-likelihood
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-cap: "The likelihood function for the plane to spot the life raft on the course it follows on its first search flight."
ggplot(Grid, aes(x = x1, y = x2, z = plane_prob)) +
  geom_contour_filled(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_contour(color = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  guides(fill = "none", color="none") + 
  coord_fixed() +
  xlab("Longitude (deg)") + 
  ylab("Latitude (deg)") 
```

The likelihood for spotting the ship is a strong function of the hypothesized ship location. Success is most likely if the ship is close to the plane's course, less likely when the ship is far from the course. 

The plane-spots-ship likelihood in `r xf("fig-plane-likelihood")` depends only on the course flown by the plane and the observational skill of the plane's crew. Although the course was selected based on the posterior distribution in `r xf("fig-ship-location")`, once the plane is on its way the likelihood function is about the plane, not about the ship. It does not factor in what is known about the ship's location. 

Once we know the outcome of the plane's observations, we can  combine the likelihood of that observation from the plane with the the current prior, that is, the posterior that takes into account the information from the direction finding radios.

The plane completes its mission, but unfortunately it does not spot the life raft. So the relevant likelihood function is for *not* seeing the ship, that is, 1 minus the likelihood plotted in `r xf("fig-plane-likelihood")`.

After the plane's fruitless search flight, the new posterior for the ship's location shows low probability for the locations where the plane would have been likely to spot the ship *if the ship had been at those locations.*   

Now we are in a position to combine all the information:

1. The initial prior before radio detection data came in. `r xf("fig-ship-prior")`
2. The likelihoods from the individual Stations' direction observations. `r xf("fig-direction-likelihoods")` (a) and (b).
3. The plane's unsuccessful search. One minus `r xf("fig-plane-likelihood")`.

The posterior distribution is based on all of (1), (2), and (3) and is calculated by multiplying the prior (1) by the likelihoods of (2) and (3). This Bayesian product of prior and likelihoods is shown `r xf("fig-ship-posterior2")`.


```{r}
#| label: fig-ship-posterior2
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-cap: "The updated posterior probability after the plane's unsuccessful search flight."
Grid$posterior <- Grid$density * (1 - Grid$plane_prob)

ggplot(Grid, aes(x = x1, y = x2, z = posterior)) +
  geom_contour_filled(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_contour(color = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  guides(fill = "none", color="none") + 
  coord_fixed() +
  xlab("Longitude (deg)") + 
  ylab("Latitude (deg)")  
```

This overall posterior has a complex shape because the plane's failing to see the ship rules out certain locations for the ship. 

Successive search flights can be arranged to target those regions in `r xf("fig-ship-posterior2")` where the probability is still high. Each unsuccessful search mission will rule out additional areas for the ship's location. A successful search mission---something we all hope for---will narrow the posterior to a very small region. When that region is so small that a rescue flight could easily spot the ship, the search is effectively over.
